content: The International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO), the International Council of Nurses (ICN), and the International Confederation of Midwives (ICM) have convened regional conferences to inform their members about the updated recommendations. Once translations of the document are available in other official UN languages, efforts will be made to ensure effective dissemination. An evaluation survey will be conducted targeting ministries of health, WHO offices, partners, professional organizations, and civil society to assess the extent and effectiveness of dissemination, evaluate the implementation of the guidance in national policies, and identify areas for further refinement and research gaps in contraceptive provision. The third edition of the Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use (SPR) includes all new, revised, and confirmed practice recommendations on contraceptive use, along with a summary of changes from the second edition. This document serves as an annex to the third edition. Recommendations for the inclusion of Sino-implant (II)® as a new method in the SPR for progestogen-only implants are based on evidence from the second edition, which included implants containing levonorgestrel (LNG) and etonogestrel (ETG). LNG-containing implants in the second edition included Norplant® (a six-rod implant containing 36 mg of LNG per rod, approved for five years of use but no longer in production) and Jadelle® (a two-rod implant containing 75 mg of LNG per rod, approved for five years of use). The ETG implant included in both the second and third editions is a single-rod implant containing 68 mg of ETG, approved for three years of use, marketed under the brand names Implanon® and Nexplanon®. For the third edition, the Guideline Development Group (GDG) reviewed evidence on a newly available LNG-containing implant, Sino-implant (II) (SI-II), which is a two-rod implant containing 75 mg of LNG per rod, approved for four years of use. The GDG determined that the recommendations for initiating SI-II are the same as those for other progestogen-only implants. A woman can start SI-II within seven days of the start of her menstrual bleeding or at any other time if it is reasonably certain she is not pregnant. Recommendations are also provided for when additional protection is needed and for women who are amenorrheic, postpartum, post-abortion, or switching from another method. The quality of evidence for these recommendations is categorized as no direct evidence, but the strength of the recommendation is strong. A systematic review of evidence on initiating SI-II identified 105 articles, none of which met the inclusion criteria for direct evidence. However, one small study provided evidence on LNG levels after SI-II insertion in 10 women during days 1–7 of the menstrual cycle, showing an initial LNG level of 28 ng/mL. Since SI-II is highly effective for at least four years of continuous use, during which serum LNG levels are lower than one week after insertion, the higher initial LNG level likely indicates effectiveness as early as one week post-insertion. The GDG also reviewed similarities between SI-II and other LNG and ETG implants included in the second edition of the SPR and concluded that there were no major differences warranting different recommendations for SI-II. The GDG based its recommendations for SI-II initiation on indirect evidence from studies on other progestogen-only implants and proxy outcomes for SI-II. Due to the similarities among progestogen-only implants in terms of safety profile, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, delivery system, and mechanism of action, evidence from other implants was extrapolated to SI-II. Additional supporting evidence from a systematic review prepared for the WHO’s Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (MEC) fifth edition noted that different progestogen-only implants exhibit similar safety profiles. The GDG also considered common barriers to safe, correct, and consistent contraceptive use and the benefits of preventing unintended pregnancies. Women’s values and preferences were integral to the process of translating evidence into recommendations, ensuring that contraceptive provision recommendations facilitate access while maintaining safety and efficacy. Regarding examinations and tests before initiating SI-II, the GDG determined that the recommendations are the same as those for other contraceptive implants. Blood pressure measurement is desirable but not mandatory before initiating SI-II, and women should not be denied access to SI-II if their blood pressure cannot be measured. Routine laboratory tests, breast examinations, pelvic/genital examinations, cervical cancer screening, and STI/HIV screening are not deemed necessary for the safe and effective use of SI-II. The quality of evidence for these recommendations is categorized as no direct evidence, but the strength of the recommendation is strong. Three systematic reviews were conducted to evaluate the necessity of examinations and tests before initiating hormonal contraception. No evidence specific to contraceptive implants was identified, but evidence from combined oral contraceptives (COCs) was considered. One review suggested that cardiovascular outcomes are worse among women who do not receive blood pressure measurements before initiating COCs compared to those who do. Another review found no evidence comparing health outcomes among women who received laboratory screenings before initiating COCs versus those who did not. A third review found no evidence comparing health outcomes among women who received clinical breast or pelvic examinations before initiating COCs versus those who did not. The GDG concluded that evidence from COCs and other progestogen-only implants can be extrapolated to SI-II due to similarities in hormonal components and safety profiles. The GDG determined that the benefits of these recommendations outweigh any potential harms and classified them as strong recommendations. Examinations and tests not necessary for determining medical eligibility for contraception may pose barriers to access. However, some of these examinations or tests may still be appropriate for preventive health care or diagnosing suspected medical conditions. Regarding the duration of SI-II use, the GDG determined that recommendations align with the product labeling, which states that the implant can remain in place for up to four years. Evidence from 11 studies indicates that SI-II remains highly effective at preventing pregnancy through five years of continuous use, although some studies show higher pregnancy rates during the fourth and fifth years compared to users of other contraceptive implants. Evidence on SI-II efficacy beyond the fifth year is limited. The GDG agreed that the evidence supports the product labeling of four years for continuous use and classified this as a strong recommendation. Ongoing studies are investigating the duration of SI-II use. For follow-up after SI-II initiation, the GDG determined that no routine follow-up is required, consistent with recommendations for other contraceptive implants. The quality of evidence for this recommendation is categorized as no direct evidence, but the strength of the recommendation is strong. Two systematic reviews and two additional articles related to follow-up after initiating contraceptive methods were identified, but no studies focused specifically on follow-up for implant users.
